routes.description: Establish that the modern West's characteristic commitments to compassion, equality, freedom, consent, and abolition are historically unintelligible without Christianity's doctrines, narratives, communities, and institutions, while allowing that Christian influence need not be exclusive or mechanically deterministic.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it identifies distinctively Christian moral ideas, shows credible mechanisms transmitting them into Western practices and institutions, and explains apparent scriptural, ecclesial, and pre-Christian counterexamples without making every Western outcome Christian by definition.

motionBridge.description: Connect the named modern Western values to an indispensable Christian historical genealogy rather than merely showing temporal coexistence or isolated Christian participation.

centralBridges.description: Identify Christian doctrines and narratives capable of generating universal dignity, concern for the weak, reciprocal obligation, and emancipation.
Trace those moral sources through communities, legal concepts, reform movements, and durable institutions into the modern West.
Account for difficult biblical texts, Christian defenses of hierarchy or slavery, and analogous pre-Christian values while preserving the claimed genealogy.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend a bounded historical standard under which inherited influence can persist despite unbelief, contestation, and later secular reformulations.
Explain why proposed material, political, or counterfactual alternatives do not eliminate Christianity's contribution to the history that occurred.

routes.description: Establish that the modern Western moral package is better explained by multiple traditions, institutional conflict, material change, oppressed groups' resistance, and secular moral development, while permitting particular and substantial Christian contributions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it distinguishes Christian contribution from Christian necessity or authorship, supplies credible independent sources and causal mechanisms for the named values, and shows that contrary biblical and Christian precedents limit any uniquely Christian genealogy.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christianity is one contingent contributor within a mixed genealogy rather than the indispensable source of the named modern Western values.

centralBridges.description: Establish that compassion, protection, equality, or related moral practices arose before or outside Christianity in forms relevant to the origin claim.
Explain modern rights and reforms through institutional conflict, self-interest, resistance by oppressed groups, technological change, and material conditions.
Use biblical permissions, exclusions, coercive implications, and competing Christian historical practices to test claims of inherent Christian development.
Separate Christian participation or institutionalization from authorship, uniqueness, necessity, and completion of modern moral principles.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require criteria that distinguish genuine Christian inheritance from retrospective selection of Christian precedents for any eventual Western outcome.
Test the genealogy against the specific modern meanings of freedom, equal social standing, bodily autonomy, and universal abolition.

sections.title: Standards for Historical Moral Genealogy
sections.rationale: The debate depends on what counts as causal inheritance: indispensable influence, unique origin, institutional contribution, or one factor among many. This section covers boundedness, falsifiability, secular reformulation, alternative pathways, and the distinction between actual history and counterfactual development.

sections.title: Compassion, the Weak, and Protective Institutions
sections.rationale: Compassion supplies a principal test of whether Christian narrative and worship generated a distinctive concern for vulnerable people and scaled it through hospitals and charity, or instead institutionalized values already present in other traditions.

sections.title: Rights, Equality, and Freedom
sections.rationale: This section addresses central named and defining Western commitments by testing proposed lines from biblical anthropology, Christian practice, canon law, dissent, and natural rights against founding-era unbelief, exclusion, institutional conflict, and social struggle.

sections.title: Gender Equality, Marriage, and Consent
sections.rationale: Gender equality and bodily autonomy test whether reciprocal Christian teachings and women's early religious roles contain a trajectory toward modern equality and consent, or whether scriptural restrictions and the limits of mutual marital authority require other developments.

sections.title: Scripture, Slavery, and Abolition
sections.rationale: Abolition is a major motion-level case because Christian scripture, churches, enslaved believers, and reformers appear within both emancipatory and pro-slavery histories. The issue tests narrative interpretation, textual permission, institutional transformation, political struggle, and causal attribution.
